ref: #root > section:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(2) > div > div:nth-of-type(1) > img
subject: not found
message: The text alternative "not found" describes something the image does not show.

patch.ref: #root > section:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(2) > div > div:nth-of-type(1) > img

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: This is the house icon at the left of the main navigation bar. In both the snapshot and the live bundle it is a plain img inside a non-interactive Box with alt 'not found'. That alt is a leftover string with no relation to the house picture, so screen reader users hear 'not found'. If the icon is decorative it needs empty alt (F39); if it means 'Início' it needs that text (F30). Either way it fails 1.1.1, as the finding says.

skeptic.label: true_positive
skeptic.rationale: This is the house icon (icon-home.svg) at the start of the main navigation, exposed as an image named 'not found'. It sits in a plain Box with no link and no click handler; the live source still has alt 'not found'. 'not found' is leftover fallback text: it neither describes the home icon nor lets AT ignore it as decoration. This is the F30 pattern, a failure whether the icon is meant to be informative or decorative.

ref: #root > section:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(4) > form > div > div > div > img
subject: Contraste
message: The text alternative "Contraste" describes something the image does not show.

patch.ref: #root > section:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(4) > form > div > div > div > img

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: This is a 19px magnifying-glass icon at the start of the search input, rendered as an MUI input adornment, and it is not interactive. Its alt is 'Contraste' ('Contrast'), which does not match what it shows: screen readers announce a 'Contraste' image inside the search form. The icon is decorative because the 'BUSCAR SERVIÇO' button gives the purpose, so it should have empty alt. As it is, the misleading alt fails 1.1.1 (F30/F39). The live bundle still has alt 'Contraste'.

skeptic.label: true_positive
skeptic.rationale: This is the magnifier icon (searchIcon.svg) inside the search field's adornment, exposed as an image named 'Contraste' ('Contrast'). It is not aria-hidden, and the live React source still renders it with alt 'Contraste'. The icon may be decorative, since the BUSCAR SERVIÇO button already conveys search, but then it should have an empty alt so AT ignores it. Instead screen readers announce a misleading 'Contraste' next to the search field. That is neither an equivalent alternative nor an ignorable decoration, so it fails 1.1.1 (F30 pattern).

ref: #root > footer > div:nth-of-type(2) > div > div:nth-of-type(2) > img
subject: Rodapé 2
message: The text alternative "Rodapé 2" describes something the image does not show.

patch.ref: #root > footer > div:nth-of-type(2) > div > div:nth-of-type(2) > img
patch.to: Brasão e nome do Estado de Mato Grosso do Sul

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: This is the footer image (an SVG from noticias.ms.gov.br) showing the state coat of arms and the words 'Estado de Mato Grosso do Sul'. Its alt is 'Rodapé 2' ('Footer 2'), a placeholder or file-style label that names neither the logo nor the text in the image (F30). If it were treated as decorative, a non-null alt like this would still fail (F39). Either way, the text alternative does not serve the image's purpose, as the finding says.

skeptic.label: true_positive
skeptic.rationale: This is the footer image: the Mato Grosso do Sul coat of arms with the words 'Estado de Mato Grosso do Sul', exposed to assistive technology as an image named 'Rodapé 2' ('Footer 2'). I checked that the crop matches the element's bounds in the screenshot. The alt is a CMS slot label, not an alternative. It is the 'placeholder text as alt' pattern of F30. If the logo is informative, the alt should carry its text. If it is redundant with the nearby 'Governadoria do Estado de Mato Grosso do Sul', it should be empty so AT ignores it. It is neither, and it is not a link, so no other name rescues it.

ref: #root > section:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(4) > form > div > div > input
subject: Ex: CNH, Matrícula escolar...
message: The placeholder "Ex: CNH, Matrícula escolar..." has a contrast of 2.07:1 with the field (#0057af6b on #ffffff). Placeholder text is text, and WCAG 1.4.3 asks for 4.5:1.
html: <input placeholder="Ex: CNH, Matrícula escolar..." type="text" class="portal195 portal180 portal199" value="">

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: The main service search input shows the placeholder 'Ex: CNH, Matrícula escolar...' in 14px bold text styled #0057AF at about 42% alpha on a white field. Sampling the screenshot gives #94B8DD on #FFFFFF, about 2.07:1, far below the 4.5:1 needed for text of this size. The placeholder is visible text that carries the only in-field hint of what to type, so 1.4.3 applies. The page has an overlay accessibility menu with contrast modes, but that does not make the default presentation conform, and nothing shows it meets G174. The live bundle still sets this placeholder to #0057AF with opacity.

skeptic.label: true_positive
skeptic.rationale: This is the placeholder of the header's service search field. In the screenshot its glyph pixels are (148,184,221) on white, which is 2.07:1 and matches the rule's figure. The text is 14px bold, so it is not large text and needs 4.5:1. The Understanding document for 1.4.3 says the criterion covers placeholder text. The field is enabled, so the inactive-component exception does not apply. I checked whether G174 could rescue it through the site's accessibility widget (acessibilidade.bundle.js). Its 'escuro' and 'claro' modes only override text color and background with !important and do not restyle ::placeholder, and 'invertido' turns the placeholder into roughly 2.5:1 on black. The widget's button also does not show in the captured screenshot. No technique I could find makes this pass.

ref: #root > div:nth-of-type(4) > section:nth-of-type(4) > div > div > div > div:nth-of-type(1) > h1
message: The heading "1237" says nothing about the content under it.

auditor.label: uncertain
auditor.rationale: This is a statistic card in the 'Indicadores' section: the number 1237 is an h1, through MUI Typography variant 'h1', and its caption 'Serviços no portal' is an h2. The matching card '1144494 / Usuários cadastrados' renders its number as a plain paragraph, which shows the heading level is used only for styling. A user moving by headings hears 'heading level 1, 1237', which does not name a topic, so G130's test fails. But the real defect is heading markup on content that is not a heading (1.3.1, F43), and the fix is to remove that markup, not to reword the heading. Competent auditors would split on also counting this as a 2.4.6 failure.

skeptic.label: uncertain
skeptic.rationale: '1237' is the big number on a statistics card under 'Indicadores', marked up as h1, with the caption 'Serviços no portal' as an h2 below it. In the heading list it reads as 'heading 1, 1237', which says nothing on its own. But visually the number is not a heading of any section. The real defect is heading markup used for a styled statistic, which most auditors file under 1.3.1. The number and its h2 caption together do convey the meaning. Whether a 1.3.1 markup misuse should also count as a 2.4.6 failure is something competent auditors split on, so I leave it uncertain.

ref: #root > section:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(4) > form > div > div > input
message: The label "Ex: CNH, Matrícula escolar..." does not say what to enter.

auditor.label: false_positive
auditor.rationale: This is the main search field. Its only visible text is the placeholder 'Ex: CNH, Matrícula escolar...', next to a magnifier icon and an adjacent 'BUSCAR SERVIÇO' submit button (G167, the button labels the field's purpose). Together they make clear what to enter: the name of a government service, with CNH and school enrolment as examples. The labelling describes the purpose, so it does not fail 2.4.6. The field does lack a persistent visible or programmatic label beyond the placeholder, which belongs under 3.3.2/1.3.1, not 2.4.6. The model had the button text in the ancestor context and still judged the label non-descriptive.

skeptic.label: false_positive
skeptic.rationale: This is the header's single-field service search. Its only name is the placeholder 'Ex: CNH, Matrícula escolar...', which shows examples of what to type: service names such as CNH (driver's licence) or school enrolment. Right next to it is the submit button 'BUSCAR SERVIÇO', with a magnifier icon at the start of the field. Per G167, an adjacent button with a clear name acts as the label of a search field, so the field's purpose ('search for a service') is described. The model had the button text in its ancestor context and still judged the placeholder alone. The real weakness is relying on a placeholder that disappears instead of a persistent label, which belongs under 3.3.2, not 2.4.6. The finding's claim that the label 'does not say what to enter' is also not accurate, since the examples do say it.

ref: #divMarcaRodape
subject: Portal Unificado da Justiça Federal da 4ª Região
message: The text "Portal Unificado da Justiça Federal da 4ª Região" has at most 3.41:1 contrast with what is behind it (#ffffff on #339999), measured from pixels because axe-core could not decide (a background image). WCAG 1.4.3 asks for 4.5:1.

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: The element is the footer caption div#divMarcaRodape, which holds the live HTML text 'Portal Unificado da Justiça Federal da 4ª Região'. It is not part of an image: the tudo_aqui.png background sits 35px below it. The live CSS (infra-local.css) sets div#divAreaGlobalRodape to color #FFFFFF on background-color #339999 and div#divMarcaRodape to font-size 17px at normal weight. Sampling the screenshot behind the text gives a solid rgb(51,153,153). White on #339999 is 3.41:1. That is below 4.5:1, and 17px regular is not large text. The packet's image crop shows only the logo area, but the full screenshot shows the text clearly, white on teal. I considered the logotype exception, since the div is named 'marca'. This is ordinary page text in the site font, a caption next to the logo graphic and not the logo itself, so the exception does not apply. The finding names a real 1.4.3 failure. The rest of the footer's white-on-teal link text fails the same way.

skeptic.label: true_positive
skeptic.rationale: The element is the footer div #divMarcaRodape. Its live text 'Portal Unificado da Justiça Federal da 4ª Região' is shown at its top, above a background image (tudo_aqui.png, positioned 35px down) that holds the logos and the 'tudo aqui.' slogan. The packet crop shows only that background, but the page screenshot shows the text in white on solid teal. The live CSS confirms #divAreaGlobalRodape is background-color #339999 and color #FFFFFF, and the div is 17px at weight 400, so it is not large text. White on #339999 works out to 3.41:1, short of the 4.5:1 that 1.4.3 requires. The background image does not sit behind the text, so the pixel measurement is not an artefact. I checked two ways it could pass. First, the logotype exception: the text is plain HTML in the same Lato face as the other footer text, not part of the logo graphic, so the exception does not cover it. Second, G174: the page has an 'Alto Contraste' toggle that turns this text white on black. G174 only works if the alternate version meets every Level A/AA criterion and can be reached through an accessibility-supported mechanism. This toggle is an <a> with no href, tabindex=0 and only a click handler (it works through accesskey but not with Enter), and nothing shows the alternate version fully conforms. So that technique cannot be credited, and the default presentation fails.

ref: #txtBuscaPortal
message: Nothing on screen tells what to enter in the field "Expressão de busca": its label is hidden from view.

auditor.label: false_positive
auditor.rationale: The element is the header search field #txtBuscaPortal. Its <label> 'Expressão de busca' is visually hidden (class LeitorDeTela), and so is the fieldset legend. Even so, the screen does say what to enter. A visible h2 'o que você procura?' ('what are you looking for?') sits directly above the field, and a magnifying-glass submit button ('Buscar no Portal') sits inside it. Together they tell sighted users that this is a site search box (compare G131 and G167). SC 3.3.2 asks for labels or instructions; it does not ask for a visible <label> element. The live page and the screenshot match. The model had the nearby h2 in its context and still claimed that nothing on screen explains the field, so this is a model error.

skeptic.label: false_positive
skeptic.rationale: The element is the portal search box #txtBuscaPortal. Its <label class='LeitorDeTela'> is moved off-screen (left:-9999px), so it has no visible text label. The claim that 'nothing on screen tells what to enter' is still wrong. In the screenshot and in the live HTML, an h2 'o que você procura?' ('what are you looking for?') sits right above the field and works as a visible prompt. A submit button with a magnifying-glass icon (input #sbmBuscaPortal, accessible name 'Buscar no Portal') follows the field in the DOM and appears inside its right edge. That is technique G167 (Example 1: a magnifying-glass search button labels the adjacent search field), which is sufficient for 3.3.2. Under 3.3.2, a label or instruction only has to be visible; it does not have to be programmatically associated (that is 1.3.1/4.1.2). The heading was in the context the checker had (headingsNear), so it judged wrongly.

ref: #sort_news_205662 > article > a > img
subject: selo_ruf_2026.png
message: The text alternative "selo_ruf_2026.png" is a file name: a screen reader reads it in place of the image. Describe what the image conveys, or use alt="" if it is decorative.

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: News-card image (the 'Ranking Universitário Folha 2026 RUF' seal) that is the only content of a link to the ranking article. Its alt is the file name 'selo_ruf_2026.png', which the browser uses as the link's accessible name. A file name as the text alternative is documented failure F30. It should describe the seal or the link purpose, or be empty with the link named another way. The same alt is still on the live page. Fails 1.1.1.

skeptic.label: true_positive
skeptic.rationale: This is the news-card image (the RUF 2026 'Ranking Universitário Folha' seal) for the 'Ranking Folha diz que UFG é a 13ª melhor universidade do País' item, and the only content of its link. Its alt is 'selo_ruf_2026.png', a file name with an extension, and it becomes the link's accessible name. It neither describes the seal nor gives the link's purpose. Even if the image were treated as decorative, a non-empty file-name alt fails, so 1.1.1 fails either way (F30).

ref: #component_110722 > a
subject: Instagram
message: The icon of this link ("Instagram") has at most 2.54:1 contrast with the pixels next to it (#ffffff on #66aad5). It is all the control shows, so WCAG 1.4.11 asks for 3:1 (G207).

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: Header Instagram link: a white Instagram glyph on a #66aad5 circle, with no visible text (the img is aria-hidden). Pixel sampling gives 2.54:1, below 3:1. The light-blue circle is the site's own choice, not something Instagram's brand rules require, and it turns dark blue only on hover. Understanding 1.4.11 (author-choice logos, Figure 27) says such a presentation is not 'essential', so the logo exemption does not apply. Fails 1.4.11.

skeptic.label: true_positive
skeptic.rationale: This is the icon-only Instagram link in the header: a white glyph on the site's #66aad5 circle, measured at 2.54:1 against the fill, with the circle also 2.54:1 against the white page. The light-blue circle is the author's uniform styling, not Instagram's brand presentation, so the logo exception does not apply (the Understanding document on author-chosen low-contrast logos). It fails 1.4.11.

ref: html > body > p > a
subject: link
message: The browser exposes this element as a link but computes no name for it: a screen reader announces only "link", not what it is for. Give it a name (visible text, aria-labelledby or aria-label).

auditor.label: false_positive
auditor.rationale:
The element is

: an empty legacy named anchor (a fragment target) with no href, no content and no box. Chrome lists it as role link, almost certainly from its heuristic for anchors with click listeners, but it is not in the tab order and nobody perceives it as a control. It is not a user interface component in WCAG's sense, and tools such as axe's link-name do not treat href-less anchors as links. Applying 4.1.2's name requirement to it is not warranted; replacing it with an id is a cleanup, not a fix for a failure. Still present on the live page.

skeptic.label: false_positive
skeptic.rationale:
The element is

, a legacy named anchor serving as an in-page fragment target. It has no href, no content, no size, and CDP lists it as not focusable (still present on the live page). Chrome maps it to role link, probably because a script attached a click listener, but users cannot see, focus or activate it. It is not a user interface component in WCAG's sense, so 4.1.2's name requirement does not apply.

ref: html > body > div:nth-of-type(3) > section:nth-of-type(1) > div > div > div > a
subject: link
message: The browser exposes this element as a link but computes no name for it: a screen reader announces only "link", not what it is for. Give it a name (visible text, aria-labelledby or aria-label).

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: This is a story card link, <a href> wrapping <article class="box box--galeria"> with a header (label.kicker + h3), text 'POLÍTICA Flávio recua e retira trecho da carta onde se declarou presidente do Brasil'. In the snapshot's CDP accessibility tree, Chrome gives the link name "" with no nameFrom, while plain-text links on the same page ('VEJA MAIS') get names from content. All 65 article-wrapping cards behave this way, and the live page still uses this markup. Chromium does not let an article descendant contribute to name-from-content, so the link has no programmatic name. Browse-mode screen readers may still read the inner text, but voice control, focus announcements that rely on the name, and link lists get nothing. This is a real 4.1.2 (and 2.4.4) problem. The fix is aria-labelledby on the h3, or the article placed outside the link.

skeptic.label: uncertain
skeptic.rationale: This is a home-page story card: <a href> wrapping <article><header><label class=kicker> + <h3>, with text 'POLÍTICA Flávio recua e retira trecho da carta onde se declarou presidente do Brasil'. Chrome's CDP tree really does give this link an empty name, as it does all 65 article-wrapping card links on the page, because Chrome does not let <article> content count towards name-from-content. Against the finding: AccName 1.2 step 2H includes the article's descendants, so the spec-computed name (and axe's, and the ACT link-name rule's) is the visible headline. NVDA and JAWS read the link's content, and the h3 inside it is reachable by heading navigation. For the finding: some pairings (Narrator, or TalkBack with Chrome, per testing of the analogous figure-in-link pattern) announce only 'link' or the URL. So this is Chrome's exposure deviating from spec-conformant markup, and competent auditors would split on calling it a 4.1.2 failure. The live page still uses the same markup.

message: The browser exposes this element as a link but computes no name for it: a screen reader announces only "link", not what it is for. Give it a name (visible text, aria-labelledby or aria-label).

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: This is a story card link, <a href> wrapping <article class="box box--galeria"> with a header (label.kicker + h3), text 'MOMENTO ESPECIAL Renner se emociona ao fazer primeira gravação e homenagear parceiro Ri...'. In the snapshot's CDP accessibility tree, Chrome gives the link name "" with no nameFrom, while plain-text links on the same page ('VEJA MAIS') get names from content. All 65 article-wrapping cards behave this way, and the live page still uses this markup. Chromium does not let an article descendant contribute to name-from-content, so the link has no programmatic name. Browse-mode screen readers may still read the inner text, but voice control, focus announcements that rely on the name, and link lists get nothing. This is a real 4.1.2 (and 2.4.4) problem. The fix is aria-labelledby on the h3, or the article placed outside the link.

skeptic.label: uncertain
skeptic.rationale: This is a home-page story card: <a href> wrapping <article><header><label class=kicker> + <h3>, with text 'MOMENTO ESPECIAL Renner se emociona ao fazer primeira gravação e homenagear parceiro Rick…'. Chrome's CDP tree really does give this link an empty name, as it does all 65 article-wrapping card links on the page, because Chrome does not let <article> content count towards name-from-content. Against the finding: AccName 1.2 step 2H includes the article's descendants, so the spec-computed name (and axe's, and the ACT link-name rule's) is the visible headline. NVDA and JAWS read the link's content, and the h3 inside it is reachable by heading navigation. For the finding: some pairings (Narrator, or TalkBack with Chrome, per testing of the analogous figure-in-link pattern) announce only 'link' or the URL. So this is Chrome's exposure deviating from spec-conformant markup, and competent auditors would split on calling it a 4.1.2 failure. The live page still uses the same markup.

auditor.label: true_positive

In the live HTML it has onclick="openNewWindow('https://impresso.correio24horas.com.br/...')" and cursor:pointer. It has no role and no tabindex, and it holds no link or button: in the snapshot its children are only an img and plain text. Chrome exposes it as a generic with a click listener, so its control role is not programmatically determinable (F59). It is also unreachable by keyboard (2.1.1). This is a real 4.1.2 failure.

skeptic.label: true_positive
skeptic.rationale: This is the footer 'Versão Impressa' block (div.versao-digital-container). The live HTML shows onclick="openNewWindow('https://impresso.correio24horas.com.br/…')" and cursor:pointer on it. It has no role and no tabindex, and there is no link or button inside it, only an img (alt 'Miniatura Jornal') and text. The snapshot's CDP tree exposes it as generic with a click listener. A script-driven control on a div with no role is documented failure F59 of 4.1.2, and it is also not keyboard operable. No technique makes it pass.

ref: html > body > div:nth-of-type(3) > section:nth-of-type(16) > header > h2
message: The heading "Asteriscão" says nothing about the content under it.

auditor.label: false_positive
auditor.rationale: The h2 'Asteriscão' is the proper name of one of the newspaper's sections. On the live site, /asteriscao is titled 'Asteriscão | Jornal Correio' and described as 'Reportagens de fim de semana do Asteriscão'. All four stories under the heading link to /asteriscao/ URLs, and a 'Veja mais' link leads to that section. The heading correctly identifies which section the block holds, much as a named newspaper supplement does. 2.4.6 asks that headings describe topic or purpose. It does not ask a section's name to summarise its stories, so I do not count a branded section title as a failure.

skeptic.label: false_positive
skeptic.rationale: h2 'Asteriscão' is the proper name of a Correio section: every story under it links to /asteriscao/… and its 'Veja mais' goes to the subscriber area. A heading that names the section its items belong to identifies that block's purpose, the same way named newspaper sections like 'Ilustrada' do. 2.4.6 does not require a section heading to summarise the mixed stories under it or to explain a brand name. Calling it non-descriptive applies a stricter rule than the criterion.

ref: html > body > div:nth-of-type(3) > section:nth-of-type(12) > header > h1

skeptic.label: false_positive
skeptic.rationale: h1 'Entretenimento' heads a home-page section whose 'veja mais' link goes to /entretenimento. The four stories under it are the 'Blank Space'/'Gossip Girl' castle auction, a singer's (Renner) emotional first recording, actor José Mayer's labour settlement and a gardening tip. The heading describes the section's topic, so 2.4.6 is met and the claim that it names a different topic does not hold.

ref: #breadcrumbs-tag-item
subject: Title
message: The heading "Title" says nothing about the content under it.

patch.ref: #breadcrumbs-tag-item
patch.before: Title
patch.after: Lista de empresas

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: h4#breadcrumbs-tag-item shows 'Tópicos Relacionados' visually, but carries aria-label="Title"; Chrome's accessibility tree gives the heading the name 'Title' (nameFrom aria-label), so screen reader users hear and see in the headings list 'Title', as with the other CMS headings on the page ('Veja Também', 'Recomendado para você' are also named 'Title'). The heading as exposed to assistive technology does not describe the topic of the related-tags section, which fails 2.4.6 for those users (an auditor could also log it under 1.3.1). The finding's claim matches what AT receives.

skeptic.label: true_positive
skeptic.rationale: The h4 #breadcrumbs-tag-item shows 'Tópicos Relacionados', but it has aria-label="Title". CDP reports its name as 'Title', taken from aria-label, and other headings on the page carry the same placeholder label. Screen readers announce the aria-label for headings, so a user moving by headings or using a headings list hears 'Title', which says nothing about the tag links under it. The visible text is descriptive. One could file the mismatch under 1.3.1 rather than 2.4.6. Still, the claim that the heading as exposed does not describe its section is a real failure for screen reader users, and no technique on the element fixes it.

ref: #tab-e0gufbx
subject: generic click
message: This element ("Viu algum erro?") listens to click, so it works as a control, but the browser exposes it as generic, with no control role: a screen reader does not announce it as a button or a link (F59). Use the native element (button, a) or give it the role of the control it is.

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: div#tab-e0gufbx.nd-tab.nd-tab-active 'Viu algum erro?' is the first, currently selected tab of the same custom tab widget (onclick NdTabs.selectTab('NDbxvlg0c','tab-e0gufbx') shows its panel and hides the other). It is exposed as generic, with no tab role, no selected state and no tabindex, so AT users get neither the control nor which tab is active. F59 applies: 4.1.2 fails. Being the active tab does not change that its role and state must be exposed.

skeptic.label: true_positive
skeptic.rationale: 'Viu algum erro?' is the other div.nd-tab in the same tab widget, with onclick="NdTabs.selectTab(...)" and a click listener on the node. I considered that it is the active tab, so clicking it does nothing at first. It is still the control that brings its panel back after the other tab is chosen, and it is a tab of the widget. It has no role, no aria-selected and no focusability, so AT users cannot tell it is a selected tab in a tablist. This is the F59 pattern and fails 4.1.2.

ref: #tab-hfexcrl
subject: generic click
message: This element ("Fale com a redação") listens to click, so it works as a control, but the browser exposes it as generic, with no control role: a screen reader does not announce it as a button or a link (F59). Use the native element (button, a) or give it the role of the control it is.
evidence: role generic · click · "Fale com a redação"

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: div#tab-hfexcrl.nd-tab 'Fale com a redação' is the second tab of a custom tab widget: the live markup has onclick="NdTabs.selectTab('NDbxvlg0c','tab-hfexcrl')", which swaps the visible nd-tab-content panel. It has no role (Chrome exposes generic), no tabindex and no aria-selected, and its container has no tablist role. A script-driven div acting as a control with no role is exactly F59, so name/role/state are not exposed and 4.1.2 fails (it is also unreachable by keyboard, a 2.1.1 issue).

skeptic.label: true_positive
skeptic.rationale: 'Fale com a redação' is one of two div.nd-tab elements in a tab widget. The live markup is <div class="nd-tab" onclick="NdTabs.selectTab(...)">, and CDP shows a click listener on the node itself. There is no role, no tabindex and no aria-selected, and no tablist role on the parent. Clicking it shows the hidden panel #container-tab-hfexcrl. A screen reader exposes it as generic text, so neither its role (tab) nor its selected state is available. I found nothing that makes it pass. This is the F59 pattern and fails 4.1.2. It also fails 2.1.1, since it cannot be focused.

message: The link text "COMÉRCIO EXTERIOR" does not match where the link leads: a page titled "Tudo sobre Mercosul | A Gazeta".

auditor.label: false_positive
auditor.rationale: Tag link in the 'Tópicos Relacionados' list, visible text and accessible name 'Comércio exterior', href /tema/mercosul/. The live page still has this mapping and /tema/comercio-exterior returns 404, so the site files its foreign-trade tag under the Mercosul topic page, which lists articles on the EU-Mercosul trade agreement (one of them carries the hat 'Comércio exterior'). The link text tells the user it leads to the foreign-trade topic, and it leads to a foreign-trade topic page with a narrower title. The wording differs from the destination title, but the purpose is determinable from the text and the user lands where the text leads them to expect; this is a taxonomy naming inconsistency, not a 2.4.4 failure.

skeptic.label: false_positive
skeptic.rationale: A tag link in the visible 'Tópicos Relacionados' list, text 'Comércio exterior', href /tema/mercosul/. The live page still has it, and /tema/comercio-exterior returns 404, so the CMS sends this tag to the Mercosul topic page. That page lists foreign-trade stories (EU-Mercosul agreement, which ES products gain in the EU), some of them filed under a 'Comércio exterior' label. A user who follows 'Comércio exterior' from a related-topics list gets a page of foreign-trade news. 2.4.4 asks that the link's purpose can be determined. It does not ask that the link text match the destination page's title word for word. Mercosul trade is part of foreign trade, so the link is not misleading. Every user sees the same text, so at most this is an editorial mapping choice, not an accessibility failure.

message: The field "Insira o CEP" asks for the user's postal code but does not identify that purpose: autocomplete="postal-code" is missing.

patch.before: <input id="13b78ea2-e40f-46c1-ac6b-97f28f48010d" class="w_100% d_inline-block px_$large rounded_$medium border_1px_solid border_$border-input-default fw_$regular bg_$background-input-default text_$text-input focus:ring_0 focus:border_$border-input-focus fo" type="text" placeholder="Insira o CEP" maxlength="9">
patch.after: <input id="13b78ea2-e40f-46c1-ac6b-97f28f48010d" class="w_100% d_inline-block px_$large rounded_$medium border_1px_solid border_$border-input-default fw_$regular bg_$background-input-default text_$text-input focus:ring_0 focus:border_$border-input-focus fo" type="text" placeholder="Insira o CEP" maxlength="9" autocomplete="postal-code">

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: The element is the text input in the header's 'Escolha sua localização' popover (placeholder 'Insira o CEP', maxlength 9), which asks for the user's own postal code 'para ver as melhores condições de frete, entrega e serviços para sua região'. That is information about the user (their location), and postal-code is one of the listed input purposes. The snapshot shows no autocomplete attribute. The live page's lazy-loaded zipcode drawer component sets placeholder, onChange, value, onKeyDown and maxLength but no autoComplete, and the field has no other mechanism that identifies its purpose. A user's CEP field without autocomplete='postal-code' fails 1.3.5, as the finding says.

skeptic.label: true_positive
skeptic.rationale: The element is the text input 'Insira o CEP' in the header location popover. The screenshot shows the popover open on load. Its copy reads 'Escolha sua localização' and asks for the CEP to show freight, delivery and service conditions 'para sua região'. So it collects the user's own postal code, which falls within 1.3.5's scope (information about the user), and 'postal-code' is in the Input Purposes list. The snapshot's attributes for the input are only id, class, type, placeholder and maxlength. I checked the live ZipcodeDialog chunk: the input gets size, placeholder, onChange, value, onKeyDown, maxLength and error props, and no autoComplete. HTML supports autocomplete tokens, so the purpose is not programmatically determinable and the field fails 1.3.5. I found no technique or exception that makes it pass. The name coming only from the placeholder is a separate 3.3.2/4.1.2 concern.

ref: #control-box-content > div:nth-of-type(2) > div > div:nth-of-type(2) > div > div > div > div > div:nth-of-type(2) > div:nth-of-type(2) > a
message: The link text "Ver todos" does not tell where the link goes, and nothing around it does.

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: The element is the 'Ver todos' link (an <a> wrapping a <button>) under the 'Os mais populares' section, after a row of category filter chips and a product carousel; it goes to the Guarda-Roupa category page. Its programmatic context is only the preceding h2 'Os mais populares' (H80), which reads as 'see all most popular', not 'see all wardrobes'. The only cue that it means wardrobes is the visually highlighted 'Guarda-roupa' chip, whose selected state is shown by colour only: the chips are plain buttons with no aria-pressed or aria-selected (snapshot and live HTML agree), and the product cards are not in the same paragraph, list item or cell as the link. Sighted users can tell the purpose, so the 'ambiguous to everyone' exception does not apply. A screen-reader user cannot determine from the link and its programmatic context that it leads to the full wardrobe category, so it fails 2.4.4. The finding's 'nothing around it does' overstates it slightly, since the visual chip does, but the claim holds for programmatically determined context.

skeptic.label: true_positive
skeptic.rationale: The element is a 'Ver todos' link (an <a> wrapping a <button>) under the 'Os mais populares' carousel. It goes to /moveis/moveis-para-quarto/guarda-roupas because the 'Guarda-roupa' filter chip is selected. I looked for context that would make it pass. Visually the selected chip and the wardrobe product cards make the destination clear. But the chips are plain buttons with no aria-pressed or selected state, in both the snapshot and the live SSR markup. The cards sit in a sibling carousel that is not in the same sentence, paragraph, list item or table cell as the link. The link has no aria-label, aria-labelledby, aria-describedby or hidden text. The only usable context is the preceding heading under H80, and 'Os mais populares' + 'Ver todos' means 'see all most popular', which does not identify the wardrobe category page. Context that exists only in unrelated sibling content is the F63 pattern, so the claim that nothing programmatically associated identifies the destination holds. Some auditors would accept the reading-order context, but WCAG's definition of programmatically determined link context does not support that. The live page is unchanged on these points.

suggestionEvidence: The model suggests: "Ver todos os guarda-roupas"

ref: #email
message: The field "E-mail" asks for the user's email address, but autocomplete="off" does not identify that purpose.

patch.ref: #email
patch.before: <input type="email" name="email" id="email" placeholder="E-mail" class="form-control" autocomplete="off">
patch.after: <input type="email" name="email" id="email" placeholder="E-mail" class="form-control" autocomplete="email">

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: This is the e-mail field of the sidebar sign-up form "Quer ficar em contato com o Oncoguia? Cadastre-se aqui", which asks for the user's own address. It has a visually hidden label "E-mail" and type=email, but autocomplete="off". The input purpose is therefore not identified as the user's email, which is one of the purposes in WCAG's Input Purposes list. type=email gives only the data format, not that the address belongs to the user, so it does not meet 1.3.5 (sufficient technique H98 needs autocomplete="email"). The live page still has autocomplete="off".

skeptic.label: true_positive
skeptic.rationale: This is the email input (type=email, name=email, visually hidden label 'E-mail') in the sidebar sign-up box 'Quer ficar em contato com o Oncoguia? Cadastre-se aqui', so it collects the user's own email address, which is the 'email' purpose in WCAG's Input Purposes list. It has autocomplete="off" (still so on the live page as of this check), so no autocomplete token identifies the purpose; the sufficient technique H98 is not met. I looked for a reason it could pass: type=email states the data format, not that the address is the user's own, and is generally not accepted as meeting 1.3.5. The field is not someone else's address or a one-off non-personal entry. The failure holds.

ref: #select2-tipo_cancer-container
subject: textbox
message: The browser exposes this element as a textbox but computes no name for it: a screen reader announces only "textbox", not what it is for. Give it a name (visible text, aria-labelledby or aria-label).

auditor.label: false_positive
auditor.rationale: The element is Select2's inner span.select2-selection__rendered (role=textbox, not focusable, read-only). It sits inside the real control, the focusable select2 combobox, and only displays the current value. The combobox points aria-labelledby and aria-controls at it. The span has title="Selecione...", which gives it a non-empty accessible name under accname step 2I. That is how axe and ACT rule e086e5 (form field has non-empty accessible name) compute the name, so the span passes. Chrome's tree in the snapshot does show name "", but the value "Selecione..." is exposed, so a screen reader would not announce only "textbox". The span is not a separate user interface component in WCAG's sense. The real 4.1.2/1.3.1 problem on this widget is that the combobox is named by its current value ("Selecione...") and not by its label "Tipo de câncer", which sits on the aria-hidden native select. The rule had the title attribute and still reported a nameless field. The live page markup is unchanged.

skeptic.label: false_positive
skeptic.rationale: The element is select2's rendering span (select2-selection__rendered). select2 gives it role=textbox and makes it read-only; it is not focusable and sits inside the focusable span role=combobox, which is the control users actually operate. That combobox exposes a role and a name. The span is not a user interface component of its own, so 4.1.2's name requirement does not apply to it separately. The span also carries title="Selecione...", which names it under accname step 2I (Rampa's own name computation gets that name; only Chrome's tree shows an empty name), and Chrome exposes its value "Selecione...", so 'announces only textbox' overstates the case. The real problem is on the combobox: it is named by its current value instead of its purpose, because the hidden 'Tipo de câncer' label is attached to the aria-hidden native select. That is a 1.3.1/2.5.3 issue, not this finding.

ref: #google_search > div > input
message: The label "Pesquisar..." does not say what to enter.

auditor.label: false_positive

The placeholder "Pesquisar..." is pushed off screen with text-indent:-9999px. What users see is a magnifier icon and the Google "Melhorado pelo Google" branding, the usual cue for a site search. Even "Pesquisar" (Search) alone would be a descriptive label for a site search field. Nothing here fails 2.4.6. The model judged the hidden placeholder and ignored the descriptive name it was given. The live markup is unchanged.

skeptic.label: false_positive

Its accessible name is aria-label 'Pesquisar no Instituto Oncoguia', its placeholder is 'Pesquisar...', and it has a magnifying-glass icon; visually the field shows the icon and a 'Melhorado pelo Google' branding image. For a search field, 'Pesquisar' (Search), especially in the full name 'Pesquisar no Instituto Oncoguia', fully describes what to enter: a site search query. The label describes the field's purpose, so 2.4.6 passes. The model's claim that it does not say what to enter is wrong.

ref: #banner-sobre-cancer > form > fieldset > div > div > span > span:nth-of-type(1) > span
message: The label "Selecione..." does not say what to enter.

auditor.label: false_positive
auditor.rationale: This is the Select2 combobox in the sidebar card. The card title "Busque seu tipo de câncer" (Search your cancer type) sits right above it, and "Selecione..." is the default value or placeholder shown inside the box. The label users see is the card title, and it clearly describes the purpose, so 2.4.6 (labels describe purpose) is met. The real defect is programmatic. The combobox's accessible name comes from aria-labelledby on its own rendered value, so it is "Selecione..." now and becomes the chosen option later. The actual label "Tipo de câncer" is on the aria-hidden native select, and the visible title is not associated. That fails 1.3.1, 4.1.2 and arguably 2.5.3, not 2.4.6. The finding treats the accessible name as the label. The live markup is unchanged.

skeptic.label: false_positive
skeptic.rationale: This is the select2 combobox in the sidebar box whose visible bold label reads 'Busque seu tipo de câncer' (Search your type of cancer), directly above the control. 'Selecione...' is the placeholder option and the current value; select2 also uses it as the combobox's accessible name through aria-labelledby. 2.4.6 concerns the label presented to users, and that label ('Busque seu tipo de câncer') describes the purpose clearly. What is actually wrong is programmatic: the visible label is not associated with the combobox, and the hidden 'Tipo de câncer' label sits on the aria-hidden native select. So screen reader users hear only 'Selecione...'. That fails 1.3.1 and 2.5.3 (name lacks the visible label), not 2.4.6.

I looked for a reason it would pass (that it is hidden, or that it is a real title) and found none that holds up. Using the photographer's name or a short description would describe the card. A heading that is present must describe its topic or purpose, so this fails 2.4.6. The grid was not painted in the full-page screenshot, but that does not change what assistive technology exposes.

Its siblings are 'Jobs and Business', 'Government', 'Public Safety', 'Education' and 'Recreation', and its href is '#'. Activating it opens the Living category submenu (Individual Services, Drivers and Transportation, Taxes, Health and Family, ...), which sits in the same list item. That list item is programmatically determined link context under 2.4.4, and the model was given its text. The purpose, opening the 'Living' services section, is clear from the link text and that context, so the claim that nothing around it tells where it goes is wrong. The real defect is a link with href='#' acting as a disclosure button without aria-expanded, which would be a 4.1.2 issue, not 2.4.4.

It only illustrates the topic the heading already names, which makes it an ambiance or eye-candy image in the sense of the W3C decorative-images guidance. Hiding it from assistive technology is an accepted way to meet 1.1.1 for decorative non-text content, so there is no failure. The model treated the sample score on the sticker as page information that the text leaves out, and that was a misjudgment. A stricter auditor might suggest a short alt as a best practice, but that is advice, not a 1.1.1 failure.

skeptic.rationale: The element is the homepage hero banner: an aria-hidden inline SVG that clips a stock photo (/images/homepage-hero-image.jpeg) into a circle, showing hands holding a sample sticker that reads 'Food hygiene rating 5 Very good'. The '5 Very good' sticker is a generic example, not a rating for any business and not content that the user needs, so the image is decorative in the sense of 1.1.1. Hiding it from assistive technology is an accepted way to handle a decorative image, so there is no failure. auditor.rationale: The element is the header search field #search-input (type=search). The text is 16px at weight 400, so it is normal-size text and needs 4.5:1. Placeholder text is visible text that tells users what to type. skeptic.label: true_positive

A headless render of the live page at 1280px shows the field visible in the header, and the darkest placeholder pixel is exactly #9fa8b1. That gives about 2.41:1 for 16px regular text, below 4.5:1. The study's full-page screenshot leaves the header out, but the snapshot gives the field visible bounds and the live render confirms it is shown. On the university's alumni pages the same footer link is also called "Connect", with the title "Connect with our alumni through news and events", and its URL redirects to this same news.aspx page. 2.4.4 lets the purpose come from the link text together with its programmatically determined context, and the preceding heading counts (H80). Read as "Alumni: Connect", the link goes to the alumni news and events hub, which is the site's own "Connect" area. The text is vague, but it does not mislead. skeptic.rationale: This is a footer navigation link "Connect" in a list (Community, Connect, Donate) under the h2 "Alumni". It goes to the alumni News and features page in the alumni "news-and-events" section. 2.4.4 does not require the link text to match the destination's title. It requires that the purpose can be worked out from the text plus its programmatically determined context, and the preceding heading counts (H80). Read with that heading, "Alumni: Connect" names the alumni engagement section. The university uses "Connect" as its own label for this section. Moreover the link carries aria-label="newsbrandsireland", which overrides the image's alt in the link's accessible name, so screen readers announce the link by its aria-label rather than reading the URL in place of the image. A URL alt is poor practice, but the 1.1.1 failure claimed here is a stricter rule than the criterion; the link's terse aria-label would be a 2.4.4 question, not this one.

subject: Every Monday
message: The text "Every Monday" has at most 2.49:1 contrast with what is behind it (#ffffff on #00b8aa), measured from pixels because axe-core could not decide (an element over or under it). WCAG 1.4.3 asks for 4.5:1.

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale:
Visible "Every Monday" text (

, 23px, weight 600) in a teal circle on The Replay promo banner. It is real text, not part of a logo. The other two "Every Monday" copies are hidden responsive variants; this one is displayed. I sampled the screenshot: glyphs #ffffff on a uniform #00b8aa fill. The snapshot reports CSS color white and the same background, and the ratio computes to 2.49:1. At 23px/600 it is at most large text if 600 counts as bold, which needs 3:1; otherwise it needs 4.5:1. 2.49:1 fails either threshold, so the finding stands, though the 4.5:1 it quotes may overstate the requirement.

skeptic.label: true_positive
skeptic.rationale: The visible desktop copy of "Every Monday" (the 15px and 18px copies are hidden at this width) is white HTML text, 23px at weight 600, in a teal circle on the promo banner for a weekly video series. The snapshot takes the foreground from CSS (#ffffff) and measures the background from pixels as a uniform #00b8aa, which gives 2.49:1; the screenshot confirms white text on that teal. Weight 600 at 23px is not large text, so 4.5:1 applies, and even the 3:1 large-text threshold would fail. It is informational text, not a logotype or incidental, so no exception applies.

ref: #navbar-IE > ul > li:nth-of-type(14) > form > input
message: The label "SEARCH.." does not say what to enter.

auditor.label: false_positive
auditor.rationale: Header site-search field: text input with placeholder "SEARCH..", aria-label "Input phrase", and a submit button named "Search" (magnifier icon), in a form with action /pa.1304. "Search" next to a search button tells users the field is for search terms, which describes its purpose as 2.4.6 requires; a search box needs no more. Separate issues could be raised elsewhere: a placeholder-only visible label (3.3.2), and the visible "SEARCH.." not appearing in the name "Input phrase" (2.5.3 Label in Name). Neither is a 2.4.6 failure.

skeptic.label: false_positive
skeptic.rationale: The site search field in the main navigation: placeholder "SEARCH..", aria-label "Input phrase", next to a submit button named "Search" with a magnifier icon, in a form that submits to the search page. "Search" plus the magnifier describes the field's purpose clearly, and a site search box needs no more to say what to enter (any phrase). 2.4.6 asks that labels describe topic or purpose, which this does. Relying on a placeholder as the visible label might raise a 3.3.2 question, but the descriptiveness claim fails.

ref: #CybotCookiebotDialogPoweredbyImage
subject: logo
message: The text alternative "logo" is a file name or a placeholder.

patch.ref: #CybotCookiebotDialogPoweredbyImage

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: The element is the img #CybotCookiebotDialogPoweredbyImage in the header of the Cookiebot consent dialog. The crop and the screenshot show it is the 'IrishCentral.' wordmark, an image of text, and its alt is 'logo'. The image tells users which site is asking for consent, and no other text in the dialog names IrishCentral (the body only says 'We and our 1090 partners'). A screen reader announces 'logo', a generic placeholder that does not give the image's text or purpose, which is failure F30. If the logo were treated as decorative, it would need alt="" to pass, and alt='logo' still fails 1.1.1.

skeptic.label: true_positive
skeptic.rationale: The element is the img #CybotCookiebotDialogPoweredbyImage in the visible Cookiebot consent dialog; the crop and screenshot show it is the 'IrishCentral.' wordmark, and its HTML has alt="logo". I looked for a reason it could pass: it is not hidden from assistive technology (no aria-hidden, the dialog is shown), it is not inside a link or next to text that names IrishCentral (its parent is a plain div, and the dialog text says only 'We and our 1090 partners'), and 'logo' is Cookiebot's generic default alt rather than an author-written alternative. As an informative image of text it needs an alternative such as 'IrishCentral'; 'logo' names the kind of image, not its content, which is the placeholder pattern of failure F30. Even if one treated the logo as decorative, a non-empty alt keeps it from being ignored (F38), so the image fails 1.1.1 either way. The dialog is injected by script, so curl of the live page cannot recheck it, but the DOM attribute in the snapshot is direct evidence.

skeptic.label: false_positive
skeptic.rationale: The page is a news article whose h1 (live HTML, and visible in the screenshot) reads 'Irish father says work colleague saved his life after stroke left him speaking gibberish', and whose body tells how Kieran O'Carroll's co-worker got him to hospital during a stroke. The title 'Irish father says colleague saved his life after stroke' is a condensed form of that headline, so it describes the page's topic and purpose and 2.4.2 is met. The snapshot hit its 5000-element limit (truncated: true) inside the Cookiebot consent dialog, whose cookie detail tables fill the whole tree; no article node was collected, h1 is reported empty, and the content text the model saw was only the consent dialog. The model compared the title with the cookie banner, not with the article.

patch.ref: #shopify-section-sections--32969212035402__footer > footer > div:nth-of-type(3) > div > div > div:nth-of-type(1) > img

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: Footer VISA logo (footer-icon-visa.svg, shows "VISA" in the screenshot). It is one of eight payment-method logos in the footer bottom bar (Visa, Mastercard, Amex, Apple Pay, Google Pay, PayPal, Maestro, Shop Pay), every one with alt="" and no adjacent text (only "(c) Lakeland Ltd 2026"), no list label and no visually hidden "We accept" text. The logos tell users which payment methods the shop accepts, so they are informative, not decoration as WCAG defines it (no information, aesthetic only). Screen-reader users get none of that information. Live HTML (2026-10-28) still has alt="". Fails 1.1.1.

skeptic.label: true_positive
skeptic.rationale: Footer payment-method logo (Visa, 40x23, alt=""), one of eight such icons (Visa, Mastercard, Amex, Apple Pay, Google Pay, PayPal, Maestro, Shop Pay), all with alt="". The crop the model saw is offset, but my own crop of the screenshot confirms the logo is Visa, as the finding says. There is no visible or hidden text such as "We accept" or a list of payment methods anywhere in the snapshot, so the logos are the only place the page says which payment methods it takes. That is information, not decoration, and alt="" removes it from assistive technology. I found no technique that would make an empty alt acceptable here. Real 1.1.1 failure.

patch.after:

https://www.lakeland.co.uk/collections/knives" id="nav-level3-view-more" title="View More" aria-label="View More Knives">

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: "View More" link in the Knives column (Cooking & Dining menu) link to /collections/knives. The desktop mega-menu column is a plain div of sibling links (a bold column-title link, eight sub-category links, then this link); there is no heading, nested list or aria-describedby, and aria-label/title are just "View More". The only programmatic context is the top-level menu list item, which holds several identical "View More" links to different collections, so it does not tell them apart (F63-type: the category is only conveyed by visual column position). The snapshot has 26 such links (13 desktop + 13 mobile drawer) to 13 collections, matching the claim; the live HTML (2026-10-28) still has 26 aria-label="View More" links. The mega-menu is opacity-0 when closed but stays in the accessibility tree and focusable, so screen-reader users meet these links. Fails 2.4.4 as reported.

skeptic.label: true_positive
skeptic.rationale: Desktop mega-menu link "View More" (aria-label and title also "View More") at the bottom of the Knives column, linking to /collections/knives. I counted the snapshot: 26 "View More" links, 13 destinations (desktop menu plus a mobile copy), so the count in the message is right. The only thing that ties this link to its column is the column title, "Knives", which is a plain link in a div (class megamenu__column). It is not a heading, the column is not a list item, and nothing like aria-describedby points to it. The nearest list item is the top-level "Cooking & Dining" item, which holds every column and its own "View More" links, so the context H81 would give does not tell them apart. The checker missed no technique (G53, H77, H78, H80, H81) that would make this pass, and the visual column grouping is not programmatically determined (F63). The live page still has the same markup. Real 2.4.4 failure.

patch.to: Download myLakeland on the App Store
patch.before: <a href="https://apps.apple.com/gb/app/mylakeland/id6474622153" target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer" aria-label="Download our App">
patch.after: <a href="https://apps.apple.com/gb/app/mylakeland/id6474622153" target="_blank" rel="noopener noreferrer" aria-label="Download myLakeland on the App Store">

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: Footer badge link to the Apple App Store ("Download on the App Store" badge). It shares the accessible name "Download our App" (aria-label and alt) with the Google Play link; nothing in the name or the programmatic context (heading "Download our App" and a voucher blurb) says which store it opens, so users cannot choose the right one for their device. Fails 2.4.4. Live HTML unchanged.

skeptic.label: true_positive
skeptic.rationale: Footer link to the Apple App Store page (apps.apple.com, mylakeland). Its only content is the store badge, and it has aria-label="Download our App". The neighbouring link to the Google Play store has the same name. The context is the same for both (heading "Download our App", text "For your latest myLakeland vouchers") and does not name the store. Visually the badges say App Store and Google Play, so sighted users can tell the two apart, but a screen-reader user hears two identical "Download our App" links and cannot tell which platform each serves. Following ACT rule fd3a94 (identical names and same context must lead to equivalent resources unless the page itself shows no difference), the two store pages are not equivalent for a given user, and the visual design shows they differ. I checked whether the purpose of downloading the app is the same either way and decided it is not enough: the platform is the part of the purpose that differs. Live page unchanged. Real 2.4.4 failure.

patch.ref: #shopify-section-sections--32969212035402__footer > footer > div:nth-of-type(1) > div > div:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(2) > a:nth-of-type(1) > img

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: Image of text inside the App Store link: the badge reads "Download on the App Store" with the Apple logo, alt="Download our App". The alt drops the store name, which is the information that distinguishes it from the adjacent Google Play badge carrying the same alt, so the text alternative is not equivalent to the image's text and function. Wording of the claim is loose (omission rather than wrong content) but the mismatch is real. Fails 1.1.1.

skeptic.label: uncertain
skeptic.rationale: The Apple App Store badge image inside the footer app link, with alt="Download our App". The crop shows "Download on the App Store". The finding says the alt describes something the image does not show. That is not quite right: "Download our App" matches the badge's call to action and the link's function, which the functional-image guidance asks an alt to give. The real weakness is an omission. The alt leaves out the store name that the image of text shows, and the other badge has the same alt, so the platform information is lost (under G94, the alt does not present the same information). Some auditors would fail 1.1.1 for that. Others would accept the functional alt and file the problem under 2.4.4 (as the link findings do). Auditors could reasonably disagree on whether this fails 1.1.1, and the stated reason does not fit, so I label it uncertain.

subject: Download our App
message: The text alternative "Download our App" describes something the image does not show.

patch.ref: #shopify-section-sections--32969212035402__footer > footer > div:nth-of-type(1) > div > div:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(2) > a:nth-of-type(2) > img

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: Image of text inside the Google Play link: the badge reads "GET IT ON Google Play" (crop and screenshot), alt="Download our App". As the sole content of a link, the alt must convey the link's function, and the essential information shown, the store, is missing; the alt is identical to the App Store badge's, so it does not serve the equivalent purpose. The finding's "describes something the image does not show" is loosely worded (the gap is an omission of the store name rather than wrong content), but the alt/image mismatch it names is real. Fails 1.1.1.

skeptic.label: uncertain
skeptic.rationale: The Google Play badge image inside the footer app link, with alt="Download our App". The crop shows "GET IT ON Google Play". The finding says the alt describes something the image does not show. That is not quite right: "Download our App" matches the badge's call to action and the link's function, which the functional-image guidance asks an alt to give. The real weakness is an omission. The alt leaves out the store name that the image of text shows, and the other badge has the same alt, so the platform information is lost (under G94, the alt does not present the same information). Some auditors would fail 1.1.1 for that. Others would accept the functional alt and file the problem under 2.4.4 (as the link findings do). Auditors could reasonably disagree on whether this fails 1.1.1, and the stated reason does not fit, so I label it uncertain.

ref: #shopify-section-sections--32969212068170__preheader > div > div > ul > li:nth-of-type(1) > a
message: The link text "Help" does not tell where the link goes, and nothing around it does.

auditor.label: false_positive
auditor.rationale: "Help" link in the top utility bar (list: Help, Find a store, myLakeland) to /pages/contact-us. That page (checked live) is titled "Contact us" and opens with Popular FAQs and customer-service contact details, i.e. it is the site's help page. "Help" describes that purpose well enough for a user to decide whether to follow it; a link need not repeat the destination's exact title. Not a 2.4.4 failure.

skeptic.label: false_positive
skeptic.rationale: "Help" link in the top utility bar (next to "Find a store" and "myLakeland") linking to /pages/contact-us. Rampa read the destination: its title is "Contact us". I fetched it: it is the site's customer-service hub, with popular FAQs (orders, delivery, returns, guarantee, account), a link to the full FAQ, and webchat, phone, email and postal contact. A link named "Help" in a utility header that leads to the help and contact hub is clear from its text alone. The model had the destination and still judged it wrong. Not a 2.4.4 failure.

ref: #SearchBar > div
message: The label "Submit" does not say what to enter.

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: Header search (Algolia autocomplete). The role=combobox wrapper and the search input are both aria-labelledby="autocomplete-0-label", a <label> carrying aria-label="Submit" that wraps the magnifier submit button (title "Submit"), so both get the accessible name "Submit" (confirmed in the snapshot AX data); the only visible cue is the magnifier icon plus placeholder "Search ...". The label presented to assistive-technology users names a button action, not what the field is for or what to enter, so it is not descriptive of the field's purpose. Fails 2.4.6 (it is also a 4.1.2/2.5.3 problem; some auditors would file it only there).

skeptic.label: uncertain
skeptic.rationale: This is the Algolia autocomplete wrapper (div role=combobox) in the header search form, with aria-labelledby="autocomplete-0-label". That label is a <label aria-label="Submit"> wrapping the magnifier submit button (title "Submit"), so the combobox and the input inside it are both named "Submit". This is a real accessibility defect: screen readers announce the search field as "Submit". The question is whether 2.4.6 is the right criterion. What sighted users see is a box with placeholder "Search ..." and a magnifier icon, which describes the field's purpose. Only the computed accessible name is wrong. Many auditors would file that under 4.1.2 or 1.3.1 rather than 2.4.6. Others count the <label> element's text alternative as the label shown to AT users, and fail it under 2.4.6. The criterion mapping is open to reasonable disagreement, so I label it uncertain.

ref: #shopify-section-sections--32969212068170__header > main-header > div > div:nth-of-type(2) > nav > ul > li:nth-of-type(3) > ul > div > div:nth-of-type(2) > a:nth-of-type(10)
message: The link text "View More" does not match where the link leads: a page titled "Cooking Pots & Pans | Induction & Non-Stick | Lakeland".

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: "View More" link at the foot of the Pots & Pans column of the Cooking & Dining mega-menu, leading to /collections/pots-pans ("Cooking Pots & Pans | Induction & Non-Stick | Lakeland"). The destination is not actually inconsistent with the link (it is the "more" of that column), so the "does not match" wording overstates it; but read fairly the claim is that the text does not convey the destination, and that holds: the name is just "View More" (aria-label and title), the column is a plain div with no heading or nested list, and the enclosing menu list item holds six identical "View More" links to different collections. Fails 2.4.4.

skeptic.label: uncertain
skeptic.rationale: "View More" at the bottom of the Pots & Pans mega-menu column, linking to /collections/pots-pans, the same URL as the column-title link "Pots & Pans". The finding says the text does not match the destination. Read literally, that is wrong: "View More" under Pots & Pans leading to the Pots & Pans collection is exactly what a user would expect, so nothing is mismatched or misleading. The element does fail 2.4.4, though, for another reason: the text is generic, and the column title is a plain link in a div, not a heading or list-item context, so the link has no programmatically determined context (the sibling "View More" findings make this point). A reader could take "does not match" to mean "does not identify", and then the claim names the real failure. Because it depends on that reading, I label it uncertain.

suggestionEvidence: The model suggests: "View More Pots & Pans"

subject: id_000000
message: The text alternative "id_000000" repeats the image's file name: a screen reader reads it in place of the image. Describe what the image conveys, or use alt="" if it is decorative.

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: Colour-filter swatch image in the Colour facet: alt="id_000000" (also its title) is the SVG's file name (id_000000.svg). It is exposed in the CDP tree as an image named "id_000000", read next to the visible option text "Black (847)". The swatch is redundant with that text and should have alt="" (or the colour name); a file-name alternative is a documented 1.1.1 failure (F30/F39). The live page still uses these alts.

skeptic.label: true_positive
skeptic.rationale: Colour-filter swatch image in the Colour facet, inside the label whose visible text is "Black (847)". Its alt (and title) is "id_000000", the same as its src file name (id_000000.svg), and the browser exposes it as an image named that string (it is in the accessibility tree even while the accordion is collapsed). The swatch only repeats the colour named in the adjacent text, so it should be alt="". As coded, a screen reader reads a file name: F30 (file name as text alternative), and also not ignorable (F38/F39 style).

message: The text alternative "124" describes something the image does not show.

patch.ref: #product-tile-lister > div:nth-of-type(1) > div > article > div:nth-of-type(2) > div:nth-of-type(2) > div > div:nth-of-type(1) > label > div > img

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: Product colour swatch image in a tile (a small circular colour/pattern sample, per the crop) with alt="124" (a colour code) and title="Black Csc Retro Logo". The accessible name is the numeric code, which neither describes the swatch nor names the colour it stands for; only the title (exposed as a description) carries the colour. A text alternative that is a code rather than an equivalent fails 1.1.1 (F30); read fairly, the finding's claim that the alt does not match what the image shows holds.

skeptic.label: true_positive
skeptic.rationale: Colour swatch on a product tile: a 24px fabric swatch image (the crop shows the product colour) that is the visible content of the label for a display:none colour radio. Its alt is "124", an internal colour code that conveys nothing about the image. The colour name "Black Csc Retro Logo" exists only in the title attribute, which is exposed only as a description and is not reliably announced. ref: #product-tile-lister > div:nth-of-type(1) > div
subject: link
message: The browser exposes this element as a link but computes no name for it: a screen reader announces only "link", not what it is for. Give it a name (visible text, aria-labelledby or aria-label).
html: <div class="a:group/product-tile a:cursor-pointer a:grid a:grid-cols-1 a:gap-0 a:w-full a:grid-rows-subgrid a:row-span-2" role="link">

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: Product tile wrapper: a div role="link" (no href, no tabindex, cursor-pointer) whose content is an <article>. Chrome's CDP tree gives it name "" (every such wrapper on the page is nameless): Chromium does not take name-from-content through article/figure/sectionheader descendants. So the browser exposes a link with no accessible name, as the finding says; Rampa's own DOM name is the concatenated tile text, but what Chrome-based AT receives is empty. A role=link component without a programmatic name fails 4.1.2 (it is also a non-focusable, nested-interactive pseudo-link). Some auditors would call the empty name a Chromium deviation from accname 1.2, but it is what users of the dominant browser get.

skeptic.label: false_positive
skeptic.rationale: Product-tile wrapper <div role="link"> (no href, no tabindex, not focusable) around an <article> holding the tile ("Mens CSC Heavyweight Logo T-ShirtSponsoredNew..."). Under accname 1.2 (step 2H) a role=link takes its name from all descendant content, so it does have a name, though a long one. Chrome reports "" only because it does not recurse through the article role. Read fairly, the "computes no name" claim is a browser artefact. The wrapper has real problems of other kinds (a link role on a non-focusable container with nested links, which touches 2.1.1 and role semantics), but not the missing name the finding reports. Each tile also holds a properly named stretched link.

message: None of the 6 tabs in this list is exposed as selected: a screen reader does not say which panel is open. Mark the current tab with aria-selected="true" (and the others with "false").
evidence: 6 tabs, none selected: Heart, Cancer, Pediatrics at Guerin Children…, Neurology & Neurosurgery

auditor.label: false_positive
auditor.rationale: The element is the vertical tablist in 'World-Class Specialty Care at Your Fingertips' (Heart, Cancer, Pediatrics, ...). In the snapshot, every tab button has aria-selected="false" and all six tabpanels are hidden (class isHidden). The screenshot shows the default image collage on the right and no tab styled as active. I read the live site's RailList component in its JS bundle. It sets aria-selected to true exactly when a tab's panel is open (f===i || t===i), and it hides a panel exactly when its tab is not selected. When a tab is activated, it gets aria-selected="true" and its panel shows. On load no panel is open, so 'none selected' is the true state, and it is exposed programmatically. The finding says a screen reader cannot tell which panel is open, but none is open. Requiring one tab to be selected at all times is an ARIA authoring-practice convention, not a 4.1.2 requirement.

skeptic.label: false_positive
skeptic.rationale: The element is the 'World-Class Specialty Care' rail list (role=tablist) with six role=tab buttons, all set to aria-selected="false". In the snapshot all six tabpanels (tabpanel-0..5) are hidden (class isHidden), and the screenshot shows the default image collage with no specialty panel open. So no panel is open, and 'none selected' is the true state. The site's RailList code (live React bundle) sets aria-selected to true exactly when a tab is activated and its panel is shown (aria-selected = open index === i; panel hidden when not open). So the selected state is exposed and kept in sync, as 4.1.2 requires. The finding's claim that a screen reader cannot tell which panel is open is wrong because none is open. Requiring one tab to be selected at all times is an ARIA Authoring Practices convention, not a WCAG 2.2 requirement.

The Understanding document for 3.1.2 describes exactly this case (alternative-language links whose text is the language's name in that language, each marked with lang) as how the criterion is met, and H58 is the sufficient technique. The proper-name and single-word exceptions do not apply: the change of language is intended. A real failure of 3.1.2.

I looked for reasons it might pass: language names are not proper names or vernacular words in English, and the Understanding document for 3.1.2 gives this case (alternative language links, each language name written in that language and marked with lang) as its example. A screen reader guessing the language from the script is not a WCAG technique. Real 3.1.2 failure.

ref: #content > div:nth-of-type(1) > div > div > div > div:nth-of-type(2) > div:nth-of-type(3) > ul > li:nth-of-type(3) > div:nth-of-type(2) > ul > li:nth-of-type(10) > a
subject: 🇸🇪 Svenska
message: "🇸🇪 Svenska" is in Swedish, but it inherits the page's language (en): a screen reader mispronounces the language's name. Add lang="sv" to the link.

patch.ref: #content > div:nth-of-type(1) > div > div > div > div:nth-of-type(2) > div:nth-of-type(3) > ul > li:nth-of-type(3) > div:nth-of-type(2) > ul > li:nth-of-type(10) > a
patch.before: <a tabindex="-1" href="https://sv.patient.info/features/eye-health/halloween-and-bonfire-night-how-to-protect-your-eyes-this-spooky-season" class="ActionBar_link__Vbi7E globalseo-exclude" data-testid="action-bar-language-dialog-link-sv">

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: This is a link in the article's Language panel whose text is the language's name written in that language ("🇸🇪 Svenska"). In the snapshot and in the live page's HTML, neither the <a> nor its <span> has a lang attribute, and the only lang on the page is lang="en" on <html>, so the text is announced with English pronunciation rules. The Understanding document for 3.1.2 describes exactly this case (alternative-language links whose text is the language's name in that language, each marked with lang) as how the criterion is met, and H58 is the sufficient technique. The panel is collapsed by default (the links have tabindex=-1), but they are exposed in the accessibility tree and shown when the panel opens, so they are content of the page. The proper-name and single-word exceptions do not apply: the change of language is intended. A real failure of 3.1.2.

skeptic.label: true_positive
skeptic.rationale: Link in the Language panel whose text is 'Svenska'. Snapshot and live HTML show no lang on the link, its span or any ancestor, on a page that is lang="en". An English screen reader voice would mispronounce it. No exception applies, and the Understanding document for 3.1.2 gives this case as its example. Real 3.1.2 failure.

ref: #content > div:nth-of-type(3) > div > div:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(3) > div > p:nth-of-type(1) > a
message: The link text "setting off fireworks" does not match where the link leads: a page titled "Managing PTSD during fireworks season".

auditor.label: false_positive
auditor.rationale: The inline link "setting off fireworks" sits in the sentence "For years, we've followed the tradition of setting off fireworks and going to..." and leads to the site's article "Managing PTSD during fireworks season". It is an editorial cross-reference: the text and the destination are about the same topic (fireworks), and with the sentence as context a user can tell it leads to related reading about fireworks. 2.4.4 does not require link text to match or summarise the destination's title. None of its documented failures (F63, F84, F89) applies, and the link is not ambiguous or misleading enough to stop someone deciding whether to follow it. The finding applies a stricter text-must-match-title rule than the criterion.

skeptic.label: false_positive
skeptic.rationale: Inline link in article prose: 'we've followed the tradition of setting off fireworks', pointing to 'Managing PTSD during fireworks season'. 2.4.4 asks that the link's purpose be determinable from its text and its programmatically determined context (the sentence). It does not ask that link text match the destination's title. The link is a topical cross-reference to a related fireworks article. Any loss of clarity applies equally to sighted readers, and that case falls under the criterion's 'ambiguous to users in general' exception. No documented 2.4.4 failure covers loose editorial link wording. The finding applies a stricter text-matches-destination rule than WCAG's.

suggestionEvidence: The model suggests: "Managing PTSD during fireworks season"

ref: #content > div:nth-of-type(3) > div > div:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(3) > div > div:nth-of-type(1) > div:nth-of-type(1) > h3

auditor.label: false_positive
