In the screenshot it sits directly above a large photo of Mr Alex Day (alt text: "Mr Alex Day, Consultant Ophthalmologist...") with a "View larger" control, and the paragraphs just before introduce him as the surgeon quoted in the article. The heading names exactly what the card under it shows, so it describes its content and meets 2.4.6. Whether a heading is the right markup for an image caption is a 1.3.1 question, not a 2.4.6 failure.

skeptic.label: false_positive
skeptic.rationale: The h3 'Mr Alex Day' is the title of an image card in the article. The screenshot shows a bordered box with 'Mr Alex Day' above a photo of him (alt 'Mr Alex Day, Consultant Ophthalmologist...') and a 'View larger' button. The heading names exactly what the card holds, and the paragraphs around it quote Day's advice, so it describes its topic. Using a heading as an image caption might be argued under 1.3.1, but it is not a 2.4.6 failure. The model misjudged content it had.

suggestionEvidence: The model suggests: "Expert Advice from Mr Alex Day"

ref: #header-menu > li:nth-of-type(4) > a
subject: More
message: The link text "More" does not tell where the link goes, and nothing around it does.

patch.ref: #header-menu > li:nth-of-type(4) > a
patch.before: <a href="#" aria-label="More" 1="" aria-hidden="false">
patch.after: <a href="#" aria-label="More options" 1="" aria-hidden="false">

auditor.label: false_positive
auditor.rationale: This is the 'More' item in the Main navigation (a href='#' aria-label='More'). It does not go anywhere: it opens a submenu. That submenu (Schools, Support Us, Venue hire, News and Stories, Projects, Our history, Shop) sits in the same list item, right after the link, in both the DOM and the accessibility tree. With the link's programmatically determined context (its list item inside nav 'Main'), its purpose is clear: it reveals more sections of the site. That meets 2.4.4. The live page has the same markup. The real problem with this control is a different one: a link used as a disclosure button, with no button role and no aria-expanded. That would fall under 4.1.2, not 2.4.4.

skeptic.label: false_positive
skeptic.rationale: This is the 'More' item (href='#') in the main navigation (nav 'Main'). It opens a submenu, and the submenu sits in the same list item: Schools, Support Us, Venue hire, News and Stories, Projects, Our history, Shop. The snapshot shows those links exposed and focusable, and the live HTML matches. Text in the same list item is programmatically determined link context under 2.4.4, and it makes clear that the link shows more site sections. The ancestor text the checker was given contained that list, so 'nothing around it does' is wrong. A link with href='#' used as a disclosure toggle without aria-expanded would be a 4.1.2 role/state issue, not a 2.4.4 failure.

ref: #h-keyword
subject: textbox
message: The browser exposes this element as a textbox but computes no name for it: a screen reader announces only "textbox", not what it is for. Give it a name (visible text, aria-labelledby or aria-label).

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: This is the header search field (input#h-keyword, placeholder 'Search'). It has an explicit <label for='h-keyword'>Search</label>. However, the theme CSS (live main.min.css: '#header .header-search .keyword-wrap label{...visibility:hidden...}') hides that label with visibility:hidden. It acts only as a width spacer behind the input. In Rampa's recording, Chrome's CDP accessibility tree marks the label as ignored (notVisible). It lists a labelledby relation from the textbox to that label, yet reports the textbox's computed name as an empty string. Chrome does not fall back to the placeholder, because a label source was found but was empty. So in the browser Rampa used, a screen reader gets a nameless textbox, which matches the finding's claim, and the live page still has the same markup and CSS. Note: the markup looks compliant on a code read, axe would accept the placeholder, and other engines may compute 'Search'. But given the name Chrome actually exposes, an auditor testing in Chrome would log this under 4.1.2. The fix is a visually-hidden (clipped) label or an aria-label.

skeptic.label: uncertain
skeptic.rationale: This is the header search field (input#h-keyword, placeholder 'Search'). It has an associated <label for='h-keyword'>Search</label>, which the theme CSS hides with visibility:hidden. I checked a copy of this markup in Edge 156 through the DevTools protocol (Chromium's accessibility API). Chromium does compute an empty name: the hidden label wins with an empty value, and the placeholder is marked as superseded. So in Chromium-based browsers the data behind the finding is accurate. But the specs say otherwise. Accname 1.2 keeps the content of a hidden label that is the root of a native label traversal. HTML-AAM falls back to the placeholder when the label gives nothing, and ACT rule e086e5 counts a placeholder as a non-empty accessible name. Under the specs the name is 'Search', and Firefox falls back to the placeholder. Screen readers usually also read the placeholder, so 'announces only textbox' is probably overstated. Whether this fails 4.1.2 or is a Chromium bug against an author-supplied label is a point where competent auditors would disagree.

ref: #content > div:nth-of-type(2) > section:nth-of-type(4) > div:nth-of-type(2) > div > div > div > article > div > div > div:nth-of-type(2) > article > a > figure > img
subject: Inquisitive child at Horniman exhibition.

auditor.label: false_positive

skeptic.rationale: This is the thumbnail inside the Membership card link, with alt 'Inquisitive child at Horniman exhibition.'. The crop the model saw shows a young child looking up curiously, in a dim gallery with lit display cases behind him. That is what the alt says. ref: html > body > footer > div > div > div:nth-of-type(2) > a:nth-of-type(3) > img
subject: Department of Arts Logo
message: The text alternative "Department of Arts Logo" is all its link holds, and does not say where the link leads.

patch.ref: html > body > footer > div > div > div:nth-of-type(2) > a:nth-of-type(3) > img
patch.to: Department of Culture, Heritage and the Gaeltacht

auditor.label: false_positive
auditor.rationale: The element is the only image inside a link, under the footer heading "Supporters", to https://www.chg.gov.ie/. That address now redirects to the gov.ie page of the Department of Culture, Communications and Sport. The alt "Department of Arts Logo" names the supporting government department, and for a supporter logo linked to its own site, naming the organisation is what tells the user where the link goes. The extra word "Logo" is redundant but does not stop the alt doing its job, so the claim that it does not say where the link leads does not hold for 1.1.1. An auditor might separately note that the alt does not match the department name printed in the image ("Department of Culture, Heritage and the Gaeltacht"), but the finding does not claim that.

skeptic.label: false_positive
skeptic.rationale: The image is the sole content of a link to https://www.chg.gov.ie/, which now redirects to the gov.ie page of the Department of Culture, Communications and Sport. It sits under the footer heading "Supporters", beside the Arts Council and Culture Ireland logo links. The alt "Department of Arts Logo" names the government department, and the link goes to that department's site. Read in context, it tells a user where the link leads: the usual org-name pattern for a sponsor logo link. The word "Logo" is extra, and the alt is looser than the image text ("Department of Culture, Heritage and the Gaeltacht"), but the finding does not make that claim. The claim that the alt does not say where the link leads does not hold up.

ref: html > body > main > article > div > section > img
subject: hidden SM_1299_0193_PhotoBySteMurray.jpg
message: This image is hidden from screen readers (alt=""), but it conveys what the text around it does not say: "Signage showing 'OIFIG NA dTICÉAD BOX OFFICE'".
evidence: Signage showing 'OIFIG NA dTICÉAD BOX OFFICE'

patch.ref: html > body > main > article > div > section > img
patch.to: The Abbey Theatre box office counter with signage in Irish and English.

auditor.label: false_positive
auditor.rationale: The element is a photo of the box office counter (alt="") placed directly under the heading "Box Office (bookings)" and above text that says where the box office is, its hours and how to contact it. The finding says the signage "OIFIG NA dTICÉAD BOX OFFICE" carries information the text around it does not, but the English signage just repeats the heading, and the Irish line is the same name in Irish. The photo illustrates the section without adding information a user needs, so treating it as decorative with an empty alt meets 1.1.1. A short alt would be nicer, but its absence is not a failure. Checked the screenshot, the snapshot order and the live HTML, which is unchanged.

skeptic.label: false_positive
skeptic.rationale: The image is a photo of the Abbey's box office counter with alt="". It sits directly under the h2 "Box Office (bookings)" and is followed by "Located in the foyer, our Box Office is found at the main entrance on Marlborough Street...", with hours, phone, email and address. The only information the finding says the photo carries is the sign "OIFIG NA dTICÉAD / BOX OFFICE", and the heading right above it already gives that. The photo just illustrates text that sits next to it, so an empty alt is acceptable under 1.1.1 (H67 / the W3C images tutorial's case for redundant or eye-candy images). The model had the heading in its context and still judged that the image conveys something the text does not. The live page is unchanged.

ref: #fullname
message: The field "Your name" asks for the user's full name but does not identify that purpose: autocomplete="name" is missing.

patch.ref: #fullname
patch.before: <input type="text" id="fullname" name="fullname" placeholder="Your name" data-name="fullname">
patch.after: <input type="text" id="fullname" name="fullname" placeholder="Your name" data-name="fullname" autocomplete="name">

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: The element is the "Your name" field (id=fullname) in the same footer mailing list form, which asks for the user's own full name. Neither the snapshot nor the live HTML has an autocomplete attribute on the field or on the form. Its purpose matches the "name" input purpose in WCAG 2.2 section 7, so leaving out autocomplete="name" fails 1.3.5, as the finding says.

skeptic.label: true_positive
skeptic.rationale: This is the "Your name" field (input type=text, id/name=fullname) in the same footer Mailing List subscribe form. It asks for the subscriber's own name, which matches the "name" input purpose. It has no autocomplete attribute in the snapshot DOM or in the live HTML, and nothing else makes its purpose programmatically determinable. The field is optional, but 1.3.5 still applies to it. This is a real 1.3.5 failure.

ref: #email
message: The field "Your email" asks for the user's email address but does not identify that purpose: autocomplete="email" is missing. Chromium's own form check flags this field too.

patch.ref: #email
patch.before: <input type="text" id="email" name="email" placeholder="Your email" required="" data-name="email">
patch.after: <input type="text" id="email" name="email" placeholder="Your email" required="" data-name="email" autocomplete="email">

auditor.label: true_positive
auditor.rationale: The element is the "Your email" field in the footer Mailing List signup form, which asks for the user's own email address. It is <input type="text" id="email" name="email" placeholder="Your email" required> with no autocomplete attribute, either in the snapshot or on the live page now. Its purpose matches the "email" input purpose in WCAG 2.2 section 7, and HTML supports autocomplete, so the purpose cannot be programmatically determined. That fails 1.3.5, as the finding says.

skeptic.label: true_positive
skeptic.rationale: This is the "Your email" field (input type=text, id/name=email) in the footer Mailing List subscribe form, so it collects the user's own email address, and "email" is an Input Purposes token. Neither the snapshot DOM (taken after scripts ran) nor the live HTML has an autocomplete attribute on the field, and the form has none either. The id/name "email" is not a mechanism WCAG accepts for making the purpose programmatically determinable. Chromium's issue for this field (FormInputAssignedAutocompleteValueToIdOrNameAttributeError) confirms an autocomplete-style name with no autocomplete attribute. HTML supports autocomplete, so 1.3.5 fails. I found no technique or context that would make it pass.
